Causal learning & simulation across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

Across 5-7 years, causal cognition shifts from "rule-of-thumb scientists" to beginning model-builders: children move from noticing confounds and running simple tests to representing small causal systems explicitly, selecting diagnostic interventions in more complex systems, and keeping basic counterfactuals consistent with their models. This is a qualitative change in how evidence is represented more than a mere speed-up. It is visible in interventional learning on multi-variable systems, in counterfactual reasoning about indirect effects, and in an emerging grasp of necessity/sufficiency and mechanistic explanation, all capacities that are fragile or task-dependent at 5 but reliably present by 7. Recent synthesis work frames this as a move toward more "depersonalized, decontextualized" causal representations that support science-like reasoning 1.

During this window, children can use their own interventions to disambiguate the structure of three-variable systems (common-cause vs causal chains) 2 and they reliably exploit temporal dependence to infer causal direction 3, abilities only inconsistently deployed at 5. Development improves both the efficiency with which children produce the interventions needed to disambiguate causal structure and the informativeness of those interventions (children increasingly resemble "idealized Bayesian learners" 2), with intervention quality serving as a significant predictor of children’s correct causal inferences 2. In general, children this age begin to integrate prior theories with new evidence in a principled way, and this integration reorganizes their exploration itself. Another study shows that 5-7-year-olds with competing "center" vs. "mass" balance theories explore the very same apparatus differently as evidence confirms or violates their priors, and they update explanations accordingly 4; younger "no-theory" children display a simpler novelty preference. This marks a qualitative shift from the 4-5 pattern (where explanation already boosts attention to inductively rich features) toward a genuinely Bayesian trade-off between prior belief and likelihood that shapes which interventions they perform next. An experiment studies children’s exploration after demonstrations (Figure) 26. The experiment compares exploration under different instructions (Figure).

Evidence evaluation becomes more explicitly meta-cognitive between 5 and 7. During this window, children begin to represent indeterminacy ("the data don’t decide") and confounding as distinct epistemic states and use that representation to guide further testing 5, 6, 7; this understanding predicts later mastery of control-of-variables strategies (i.e holding all variables constant except for the variable being investigated) in the upper-elementary years 8 and couples to more skeptical, evidence-seeking behavior: compared with 4-5-year-olds, 6-7-year-olds are more likely to interrogate surprising claims, ask for missing evidence, and propose targeted checks, rather than accepting assertions at face value 9. A 2026 longitudinal study tests interpretation of confounded evidence (Figure) 25. The study also tests selection of causal experiments (Figure).

Explanatory practice also shifts from teleological defaults toward mechanism. Classic findings show broad "promiscuous teleology" (i.e describing phenomena according to their functions instead of the causes by which they arise) in younger children 10, but by 6-7 most children reliably favor mechanistic over merely functional or categorical explanations when both are available 11, and they begin to privilege informants who know underlying mechanisms 12. This mechanistic tilt supports better causal generalization and more adult-like evaluation of explanations as evidential arguments.

There is parallel growth in reasoning about necessity and sufficiency. Compared with five-year-olds, seven-year-olds are far more likely to treat a factor as necessary only when removing it abolishes the effect, and as sufficient only when its presence produces the effect across relevant conditions, an explicit logical framing that supports correct diagnoses in multi-cause settings and reduces over-attribution to single salient causes 13. Sensitivity to causal complexity (e.g., recognizing when multiple interacting causes must be considered or when expert help is needed to decompose a system) also becomes measurable around this age 14.

Counterfactual reasoning undergoes substantial maturation across this window. Recent research using sufficiently simple and clear physical causation tasks finds that 4- and 5-year-olds can demonstrate mature counterfactual reasoning in over-determined scenarios (where two blocks both make a box light up), with four-year-olds answering correctly significantly more often than chance and five-year-olds performing nearly perfectly when asked to mentally remove one block and predict the effect 15. Five-year-olds can entertain simple "what-ifs," (including in singly-determined scenarios like "Susie walked into the house with muddy shoes; would the floor be dirty if she did not walk into the house?" or in singly-determined physical tasks 16 which can be solved with basic conditional reasoning 17) but they often fail when complexity increases or when a change propagates through a dynamic system; by seven, children see higher success rates in more complex tasks 16, 18 and begin to accurately project both direct and indirect consequences of hypothetical changes (for example, removing a species from a food chain and predicting downstream effects 19). This counterfactual upgrade reorganizes social evaluation: by 6-7, children experience and use counterfactual emotions (regret/relief) to guide choices and learning 20, 21, and they increasingly weight whether an agent "could have done otherwise," judging benevolence more positively when helpful acts reflect choice rather than constraint 22. Related work on developing intuitions of free will shows that around this age children explicitly endorse the idea that agents can select among alternatives, aligning with their counterfactual social judgments 23. Overall, seven-year-olds see substantial improvements on tasks probing counterfactual simulation and are starting to project indirect downstream effects in dynamic systems; their success does, however, remain fragile and highly task-dependent, with performance dropping quickly as complexity or hidden constraints continue to increase 24, 17.

Overall we can say that, by seven, the foundational architecture for scientific reasoning is largely in place. What began at five as fragile, context-dependent hypothesis testing has crystallized into an integrated causal inference engine: children now maintain explicit models of multi-variable systems, run diagnostic interventions to disambiguate structure, simulate counterfactual trajectories through those models, and represent epistemic states like indeterminacy and confounding that guide further evidence-seeking. This is a qualitative shift in representation, from perceptually-bound heuristics towards abstract, depersonalized models that can be interrogated, updated, and applied across contexts. The result is a reasoning system that is beginning to look strikingly Bayesian: priors shape exploration, evidence is weighed mechanistically rather than teleologically, and necessity/sufficiency logic replaces simple association.
